coding.subject: Coding
coding.title: Count warship groups (number of islands)
coding.question:
A sea map is a grid of R rows and C columns. Each cell is 1 (part of a warship) or 0 (water). Two warship cells belong to the same group if they touch up, down, left or right (not diagonally). Count the number of warship groups.
Example: the grid
11000
11000
00100
00011
has 3 groups.
coding.input_format:
Line 1: two integers R and C.
Next R lines: a string of C characters, each 0 or 1.
coding.output_format: One integer: the number of groups.
coding.starter_code:
import sys
data = sys.stdin.read().split()
r, c = int(data[0]), int(data[1])
grid = data[2:2 + r]
# TODO: write your logic here
print(0)
hints: Each time you find an unvisited 1, you have found a new group.
From that cell, visit every connected 1 with BFS or DFS and mark it as visited.
coding.explanation: Scan every cell. On an unvisited 1, add one to the count and flood fill its whole group with BFS, turning cells to 0. Each cell is visited once, so time is O(R * C).

coding.subject: Coding
coding.title: Minimum coins to make an amount
coding.question:
You have coins of M different values and an unlimited number of each. Find the minimum number of coins needed to make exactly the amount A. If it is not possible, print -1.
Example: coins 1 2 5 and A = 11 needs 3 coins (5 + 5 + 1).
coding.input_format:
Line 1: two integers M and A.
Line 2: M distinct coin values.
coding.output_format: One integer: the minimum number of coins, or -1.
coding.starter_code:
import sys
data = sys.stdin.read().split()
m, amount = int(data[0]), int(data[1])
coins = list(map(int, data[2:2 + m]))
# TODO: write your logic here
print(-1)
coding.solution:
import sys
data = sys.stdin.read().split()
m, amount = int(data[0]), int(data[1])
coins = list(map(int, data[2:2 + m]))
INF = float("inf")
dp = [0] + [INF] * amount
for x in range(1, amount + 1):
    for c in coins:
        if c <= x and dp[x - c] + 1 < dp[x]:
            dp[x] = dp[x - c] + 1
print(dp[amount] if dp[amount] != INF else -1)
hints: Greedy (always take the biggest coin) fails for coins 1 3 4 and amount 6.
dp[x] = 1 + min(dp[x - c]) over all coins c <= x.
coding.explanation: dp[x] is the fewest coins for amount x, with dp[0] = 0. Build it from 1 to A using every coin. If dp[A] is still infinite, print -1. Time O(M * A).
coding.label: AI practice

coding.subject: Coding
coding.title: Rotate an array to the right
coding.question:
Given an array of N integers and a number K, rotate the array to the right by K steps and print it. In one step the last element moves to the front.
Example: 1 2 3 4 5 rotated right by 2 gives 4 5 1 2 3.
coding.input_format:
Line 1: two integers N and K.
Line 2: N integers.
coding.output_format: One line: the rotated array, values separated by single spaces.
coding.starter_code:
import sys
data = sys.stdin.read().split()
n, k = int(data[0]), int(data[1])
a = list(map(int, data[2:2 + n]))
# TODO: write your logic here
print(*a)
coding.solution:
import sys
data = sys.stdin.read().split()
n, k = int(data[0]), int(data[1])
a = data[2:2 + n]
k %= n
print(" ".join(a[n - k:] + a[:n - k]))
hints: Rotating by N steps gives back the same array, so use K mod N.
The last K elements come first, then the rest.
coding.explanation: Reduce K to K mod N. The answer is the last K elements followed by the first N - K elements. Time O(N).

coding.subject: Coding
coding.title: Minimum railway platforms
coding.question:
N trains stop at a station. Train i arrives at time arr[i] and leaves at time dep[i] (24-hour times written as HHMM numbers, for example 930 means 9:30). A platform can hold one train at a time. If a train arrives at the same minute another train leaves, they still need different platforms. Find the minimum number of platforms so that no train waits.
Example: arrivals 900 940 950 1100 1500 1800 and departures 910 1200 1120 1130 1900 2000 need 3 platforms.
coding.input_format:
Line 1: integer N.
Line 2: N arrival times.
Line 3: N departure times (dep[i] >= arr[i]).
coding.output_format: One integer: the minimum number of platforms.
coding.starter_code:
import sys
data = sys.stdin.read().split()
n = int(data[0])
arr = list(map(int, data[1:1 + n]))
dep = list(map(int, data[1 + n:1 + 2 * n]))
# TODO: write your logic here
print(1)
coding.solution:
import sys
data = sys.stdin.read().split()
n = int(data[0])
arr = sorted(map(int, data[1:1 + n]))
dep = sorted(map(int, data[1 + n:1 + 2 * n]))
i = j = cur = best = 0
while i < n:
    if arr[i] <= dep[j]:
        cur += 1
        best = max(best, cur)
        i += 1
    else:
        cur -= 1
        j += 1
print(best)
hints: Walk through events in time order: an arrival adds a train, a departure removes one.
coding.explanation: After sorting both lists, merge them like in merge sort. An arrival at or before the next departure needs one more platform; otherwise a train has left. The largest count seen is the answer. Time O(N log N).
coding.label: AI practice
coding.source_note: Written for practice on Infosys's reported coding topics

coding.subject: Coding
coding.title: Shortest path in a maze
coding.question:
A maze is a grid of R rows and C columns. '.' is an open cell and '#' is a wall. You start at the top-left cell and want to reach the bottom-right cell. In one step you can move up, down, left or right into an open cell. Print the minimum number of steps needed, or -1 if the target cannot be reached. If the start or the target is a wall, print -1.
Example: in the 3 x 3 maze
..#
#..
#..
the shortest path takes 4 steps.
coding.input_format:
Line 1: two integers R and C.
Next R lines: a string of C characters, each '.' or '#'.
coding.output_format: One integer: the minimum number of steps, or -1.
coding.starter_code:
import sys
data = sys.stdin.read().split()
r, c = int(data[0]), int(data[1])
grid = data[2:2 + r]
# TODO: write your logic here
print(-1)
coding.solution:
import sys
from collections import deque
data = sys.stdin.read().split()
r, c = int(data[0]), int(data[1])
g = data[2:2 + r]
if g[0][0] == "#" or g[r - 1][c - 1] == "#":
    print(-1)
else:
    dist = [[-1] * c for _ in range(r)]
    dist[0][0] = 0
    q = deque([(0, 0)])
    while q:
        x, y = q.popleft()
        for nx, ny in ((x + 1, y), (x - 1, y), (x, y + 1), (x, y - 1)):
            if 0 <= nx < r and 0 <= ny < c and g[nx][ny] == "." and dist[nx][ny] == -1:
                dist[nx][ny] = dist[x][y] + 1
                q.append((nx, ny))
    print(dist[r - 1][c - 1])
hints: BFS explores cells in order of distance, so the first time you reach a cell is the shortest way.
Keep a distance grid filled with -1 for unvisited cells.
coding.explanation: Run BFS from the top-left cell over open cells, recording the distance of each cell when it is first reached. The distance of the bottom-right cell is the answer (-1 if never reached). Time O(R * C).

coding.subject: Coding
coding.title: Longest common subsequence
coding.question:
Given two strings A and B of lowercase letters, find the length of their longest common subsequence. A subsequence keeps the order of characters but may skip some of them.
Example: for A = abcde and B = ace the answer is 3 (ace).
coding.input_format:
Line 1: string A.
Line 2: string B.
coding.output_format: One integer: the length of the longest common subsequence.
coding.constraints:
1 <= length of A, B <= 1000
Only lowercase English letters.
coding.starter_code:
a = input().strip()
b = input().strip()
# TODO: write your logic here
print(0)
hints: dp[i][j] = LCS of the first i letters of A and the first j letters of B.
If the last letters match, add 1 to dp[i-1][j-1]; otherwise take the better of dropping one letter.
coding.explanation: Fill a 2D table: equal letters extend the diagonal value by 1, otherwise take max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]). Only the previous row is needed. Time O(|A| * |B|).
